title: Forty Things I've Learned So Far
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: On his fortieth birthday, one day before Leap Day catches up with the calendar, Stuart marks the milestone by listing forty things he's learned across a teaching career that began at twenty-eight. The list ranges widely: practical classroom wisdom, such as setting test dates at the start of a unit and filming yourself teaching to work on authoritative teacher presence first, professional-development philosophy such as reading three important PD books five times each rather than fifteen once, and reflections on identity, ego, and burnout, including the idea that teaching is dangerous for people with large egos but can also be the thing that right-sizes an inflated ego. Several entries return to his core conviction that the point of school is to promote students' long-term flourishing through mastery of course material, and that character and soft skills develop mostly as a byproduct of doing hard academic work rather than being taught directly. The piece closes on a note about ordinary life: the routine weeknights after an ordinary school day are, in his view, the real stuff of life, not a placeholder for it.
points: Stuart's PD philosophy: rather than reading fifteen books once, read the three most important ones five times each, annotating and experimenting as you go — he credits Schmoker's Focus and Willingham's Why Don't Students Like School? as most formative for his own practice.

The camera and the stopwatch are, in his view, the two most useful pieces of teacher-improvement technology, and authoritative teacher presence is the first skill to target once you start watching yourself on film.

On ego: teaching is dangerous for people with large egos, like an alcoholic working at a bar, but can also be the career that most effectively cuts an inflated ego down to size, if the teacher lets it.

He reframes character and soft-skill development as a byproduct of rigorous academic work — students build resilience and character mainly by doing hard things, not through standalone character curricula.
The closing entry reframes normal life — the routine weeknights after an ordinary school day — as the actual substance of a teaching life, not a gap between more meaningful events.
quotes: Being an average lesson planner with an expert understanding of student motivation is better than being an expert lesson planner with an average understanding of student motivation. But the goal in a teaching career is to develop expertise in both.

The two most useful pieces of technology for getting better as a teacher are the camera and the stopwatch. The camera — for filming segments of your lesson and watching yourself afterwards. The stopwatch — for timing segments of your lesson to keep yourself honest about how you use time.
There are too many PD books. Rather than trying to read fifteen books once each, try to read the three most important ones five times each — annotating and discussing and experimenting as you go.
Teaching is a dangerous job for folks with large egos. It's like an alcoholic working at a bar. If you've got ego problems, start working to get to the bottom of those. Today's a good day to start.
Teaching is a beautiful job for folks with large egos. If you let it, teaching can be a great right-sizer of the teacher's ego.
The best teachers tend to have the best lives. Neglect your life outside of school (family, health, friendships) at your peril. I've learned this the hard way.

Those week nights when you're living your normal and routine life after having worked a normal and routine day at school? That is the real stuff of life. The bulk of your actual life — that's what's happening on those normal days.
